articles.title: Designing a modular, 3D-printable ROV
articles.summary: How a finite printer envelope shaped Stingray’s wing and chassis architecture.
sections: The design constraint

Stingray is a stingray-inspired underwater robot concept. The first prototype is intended to be printable on my Bambu Lab A1, which has a 256 × 256 × 256 mm build volume. Full-size body and wing geometry must therefore be split into manageable segments.
Designing for assembly

The mechanical plan uses built-in attachment features to avoid post-print drilling, separate upper and lower body sections, and dedicated space for electronics. A previously generated parts manifest records candidate pieces inside the printer envelope. A bounding-box check is not evidence of slicer fit, joint strength or assembly accuracy.
What comes next
I will measure representative joints and verify fit before committing to full-size assemblies. Mechanical design, buoyancy, sealing and structural verification remain separate milestones.

articles.title: PETG, PETG-CF and the reality of prototyping
articles.summary: Material selection is a trade-off between repeatability, print quality and eventual performance.
sections: A practical baseline

I initially explored carbon-fiber-filled PETG, using a 0.6 mm hardened-steel nozzle as the current printer baseline. Earlier experiments with PETG-CF produced stringing and quality issues. Regular PETG gave better qualitative results and became the practical prototype material.
A new failure mode

The November wing-print failures were in regular PETG. The photographs show defects concentrated around supported features; the cause is still under investigation. This matters because changing filament alone does not establish a reliable manufacturing process.
A measured approach

Future trials will preserve the slicer profile, orientation, filament, support geometry, print time, waste and dimensions. Small coupons can isolate variables before repeating a much larger print. No material has yet been validated for the intended underwater application.

articles.title: Planning the onboard electronics
articles.summary: A proposed Raspberry Pi and Blue Robotics control architecture under a prototype budget.
sections: Architecture

The intended architecture uses a Raspberry Pi as the onboard computer and a Blue Robotics controller. The control and compute hardware must fit within the mechanical design, along with power electronics, wiring and protected enclosures.
Budget and trade-offs

I set an approximate $800 prototype budget during the initial electronics planning. That is a target, not a documented purchase total. It will guide the bill of materials and prioritization of essential functions.
Verification gates
Exact component models, wiring, enclosure geometry, power budget and propulsion configuration still need confirmation. Bench and leak testing must precede any powered underwater trials.

articles.title: Prototype first: an underwater robot for marine cleanup
articles.summary: The environmental purpose behind Stingray and the path from prototype to a potential cleanup service.
sections: Mission

Stingray begins with a simple ambition: develop robotic tools that can contribute to a cleaner marine environment. An eventual service model, rather than selling robots, is the direction I am exploring.
Prototype before business
The immediate goal is to build and test a functioning prototype. A capable vehicle, a safe deployment method and a measurable debris-recovery task must come before any commercial claims.
Longer-term exploration
A separate ocean-exploration submersible is a longer-term idea. For now, the engineering journal will record experiments, successes, setbacks and decisions as the prototype develops.

logs.title: Failed prints: PETG wing segment
logs.summary: Photographic evidence of a rejected regular-PETG wing print, with defects concentrated around supported features.
sections: Activity
Documented rejected Stingray wing-segment prints in regular PETG. The date is the date of this log; exact print dates and slicer profiles are not yet confirmed.
Observations

A mostly formed panel with mounting tabs is visible, alongside a rough supported edge, loose filament and incomplete-looking local geometry. Several tree-support branches are detached, but the photographs cannot establish whether they broke during printing or afterward.
Working hypothesis

The support and overhang region is the first area to investigate. Support contact, motion, bridging or extrusion may be involved; none is confirmed. This regular-PETG failure is distinct from earlier PETG-CF print-quality issues.
Decision and next experiment

Reject the affected parts for assembly. Capture the exact segment identifier, nozzle, orientation and slicer settings. Test representative wing geometry with one variable changed at a time, and record print time, material waste and dimensional results.

logs.title: Recurring print failures: refining print preparation
logs.summary: Repeated spaghetti failures prompted a new build-plate cleaning routine and the purchase of a spool dryer.
sections: Activity
After multiple unsuccessful Stingray prints like the one photographed here, I started washing the build plate with soap before each print and purchased a spool dryer to improve print quality.
Observations

The photograph shows one example of a recurring failure: a partly formed white curved component beside a large mass of loose extruded filament, commonly described as a spaghetti failure. The exact failure count, component, material, settings and layer at failure are not yet recorded.
Process improvements

Routine plate cleaning and the purchase of a spool dryer followed the repeated failures. The dryer’s settings, use and effectiveness have not yet been established. Neither corrective action has yet been validated by documented successful repeat prints.
Working hypothesis and next experiment

The failure is consistent with extrusion continuing after loss of part or support stability. Bed adhesion, support failure and filament condition are possible factors, not confirmed causes. Record the exact part and material, first-layer result, drying conditions and failure layer. Repeat a representative test while changing one variable at a time.
